questions.prompt: Which layer of a typical clean architecture should have no external dependencies?
questions.explanation: The domain layer holds pure types and business rules and depends on nothing else.

questions.prompt: A frontend engineer only needs to know how to write JavaScript — networking and browsers are out of scope.
questions.explanation: Understanding how browsers render pages and how the network works is core frontend knowledge.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a feature-based folder structure?
options: It reduces the number of files in a project
Each feature is a self-contained vertical slice, easier to reason about and remove
It avoids the need for TypeScript
It removes the need for a router
questions.explanation: Vertical slices keep related components, hooks, and state together, making features easier to maintain.

questions.prompt: YAGNI stands for 'You Aren't Gonna Need It' and encourages avoiding speculative, unused functionality.
questions.explanation: YAGNI keeps codebases lean by discouraging building for hypothetical future requirements.

questions.prompt: What does DNS primarily do?
options: Encrypts traffic between client and server
Translates domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS resolves human-readable domain names to the IP addresses machines use to route traffic.

questions.prompt: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt data exchanged between a browser and a server.
questions.explanation: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is what turns plain HTTP into encrypted HTTPS.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code range indicates a client error?
questions.explanation: 4xx codes (like 404 Not Found) indicate the client's request was malformed or invalid.

questions.prompt: A single IP address can only ever be associated with one domain name.
questions.explanation: Many domain names can share a single IP address, especially with virtual hosting and CDNs.

questions.prompt: What does 'await' do inside an async function?
options: Immediately throws an error if the promise is pending
Pauses execution of that function until the promise settles
Converts a synchronous function into an async one
questions.explanation: await pauses the async function's execution until the awaited promise resolves or rejects.

questions.prompt: The JavaScript event loop allows non-blocking I/O despite JavaScript being single-threaded.
questions.explanation: The event loop hands off async work and processes callbacks/microtasks without blocking the main thread.

questions.prompt: Which method runs multiple promises in parallel and resolves when all of them succeed?
questions.explanation: Promise.all() waits for every promise to resolve, or rejects as soon as one rejects.

questions.prompt: Microtasks (like promise callbacks) run before the next macrotask (like a setTimeout callback) in the event loop.
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is fully drained before the event loop moves on to the next macrotask.

questions.prompt: What does the Fetch API return?
options: A Promise that resolves to a Response
questions.explanation: fetch() is promise-based; you await it to get a Response object, then parse the body separately.

questions.prompt: What does calling the setter function from useState trigger?
options: A re-render of the component (scheduled by React)
questions.explanation: Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new state value.

questions.prompt: State updates in React are guaranteed to be applied synchronously, immediately after the setter call.
questions.explanation: React often batches updates, so the new state isn't necessarily reflected until the next render.

questions.prompt: When should you use the functional updater form, setCount(c => c + 1)?
options: When the new state depends on the previous state
questions.explanation: The functional form avoids stale closures when the next state depends on the current one.

questions.prompt: You can call useState conditionally inside an if statement as long as it's at the top of the component.
questions.explanation: Hooks must be called unconditionally, in the same order, on every render.

questions.prompt: What is a design token?
options: A named, platform-agnostic value like a color or spacing unit
questions.explanation: Design tokens store visual values (colors, spacing, typography) as reusable, named variables.

questions.prompt: A component variant refers to a different visual style or state of the same underlying component.
questions.explanation: Variants (e.g. primary/secondary buttons) share structure but differ in styling or behavior.

questions.prompt: Why use an 8px spacing scale instead of arbitrary pixel values?
options: It creates visual consistency and makes spacing decisions faster
questions.explanation: A consistent base unit keeps spacing predictable and easy to reason about across a UI.

questions.prompt: What does 'git rebase' do differently from 'git merge'?
options: It replays commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history
It only works on remote branches
questions.explanation: Rebase re-applies your commits on top of another base, avoiding a merge commit and keeping history linear.

questions.prompt: 'git stash' permanently discards your uncommitted changes.
questions.explanation: git stash temporarily shelves changes so you can bring them back later with git stash pop.

questions.prompt: Which command moves a file from the working directory into the staging area?
questions.explanation: git add stages changes so they'll be included in the next commit.

questions.prompt: A detached HEAD state means you're not on any branch and new commits could be lost if you switch branches without saving them.
questions.explanation: In detached HEAD, commits aren't attached to a branch reference, so they can become unreachable.

questions.prompt: In the dependency rule of clean architecture, dependencies should point:
options: In any direction, it doesn't matter
questions.explanation: Inner layers (domain) should never depend on outer layers (UI, infrastructure).

questions.prompt: Isolating localStorage access behind a single infrastructure module makes it easier to later swap in a remote backend.
questions.explanation: When only one module touches storage, swapping the implementation doesn't require touching UI or application code.

questions.prompt: What's a key risk of premature architectural planning?
options: Over-engineering for requirements that may never materialize
questions.explanation: Planning too far ahead for hypothetical needs can add complexity that never pays off — the essence of violating YAGNI.

questions.prompt: Why is storing a JWT in localStorage generally riskier than an httpOnly cookie?
options: localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript on the page, making it vulnerable to XSS
Cookies can't be sent cross-origin at all
questions.explanation: An httpOnly cookie can't be read by JavaScript, which limits the damage a successful XSS attack can do.

questions.prompt: OAuth is primarily an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol by itself.
questions.explanation: OAuth grants access to resources; OpenID Connect layers authentication semantics on top of it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a refresh token?
options: To immediately log the user out
To obtain a new access token without requiring the user to log in again
To replace the need for HTTPS
questions.explanation: Refresh tokens let a client silently obtain new short-lived access tokens after the old one expires.

questions.prompt: Protected routes in a single-page app provide real security on their own, without any server-side checks.
questions.explanation: Client-side route guards are a UX convenience — actual security must be enforced by the server/API.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters rows before any grouping happens?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation; HAVING filters after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have matching values in both joined tables.
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN excludes rows without a match on either side, unlike LEFT/RIGHT/FULL joins.

questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee?
options: Values in the column can repeat
Each value in the column uniquely identifies a row and cannot be NULL
The table can have multiple primary keys with different names
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and implicitly disallows NULL values.

questions.prompt: Normalizing a database schema means intentionally duplicating data across tables to speed up reads.
questions.explanation: Normalization reduces redundancy by splitting data into related tables — the opposite of duplication.

questions.prompt: Which HTML element represents the most important heading on a page?
questions.explanation: <h1> is the highest-level heading; <title> is metadata, not a visible heading.

questions.prompt: Semantic HTML elements like <article>, <nav>, and <section> improve accessibility by conveying meaning to assistive technologies.
questions.explanation: Semantic tags expose implicit ARIA roles, helping screen readers navigate the page structure.

questions.prompt: Which attribute on a <label> element associates it with a form control?
questions.explanation: The 'for' attribute must match the input's id to programmatically associate the label.

questions.prompt: Which CSS property is used to set the space between an element's content and its border?
questions.explanation: Padding is the inner space between content and border; margin is the outer space outside the border.

questions.prompt: The CSS box model consists of content, padding, border, and margin layers.
questions.explanation: These four layers, from inside out, define the total space an element occupies.

questions.prompt: Which display value makes an element behave like a flexible container?
questions.explanation: display: flex enables the Flexbox layout model on the element's children.

questions.prompt: Which method selects a single element by its ID?
questions.explanation: getElementById returns the element with the matching id attribute, or null.

questions.prompt: A NodeList returned by querySelectorAll is always live — it updates automatically when the DOM changes.
questions.explanation: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList; only getElementsByClassName/TagName return live collections.

questions.prompt: Which method adds a child element as the last child of a parent?
questions.explanation: appendChild inserts the node as the last child of the parent element.

questions.prompt: Event bubbling means an event fired on a child element also triggers on its ancestors.
questions.explanation: In the bubbling phase, events propagate upward from the target to the document root.

questions.prompt: Which operator checks both value and type equality?
questions.explanation: Strict equality (===) compares value and type without coercion; == performs type coercion.

questions.prompt: In JavaScript, 'let' declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned.
questions.explanation: let is block-scoped and reassignable; const is block-scoped but not reassignable.

questions.prompt: What does 'typeof null' return in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: This is a well-known JavaScript quirk — typeof null returns 'object' due to a legacy implementation detail.

questions.prompt: Arrow functions have their own 'this' binding separate from the enclosing scope.
questions.explanation: Arrow functions inherit 'this' from the enclosing lexical scope; they don't bind their own.

questions.prompt: How do you access a property named 'key' on an object 'obj' using bracket notation?
questions.explanation: Bracket notation obj['key'] works for any property name, including those with spaces or special characters.

questions.prompt: Every JavaScript object has a prototype, which it inherits properties and methods from.
questions.explanation: Objects inherit from their prototype via the prototype chain, up to Object.prototype.

questions.prompt: What keyword is used to define a class in modern JavaScript?
questions.explanation: ES6 introduced the 'class' keyword as syntactic sugar over the prototype-based inheritance system.

questions.prompt: The 'extends' keyword allows a class to inherit from another class.
questions.explanation: extends creates a subclass that inherits methods and properties from its parent class.

questions.prompt: Where are primitive values stored during execution?
questions.explanation: Primitives are stored on the call stack along with function frames and references.

questions.prompt: When you assign an object to a new variable, the object itself is copied.
questions.explanation: Objects are passed by reference — only the reference to the heap-allocated object is copied.

questions.prompt: What mechanism automatically frees memory that is no longer referenced?
questions.explanation: JavaScript uses garbage collection (typically mark-and-sweep) to reclaim unreachable memory.

questions.prompt: A shallow copy duplicates nested objects so changes to the copy don't affect the original.
questions.explanation: A shallow copy only copies the top level — nested objects are still shared by reference.

questions.prompt: Which hook lets you perform side effects after render?
questions.explanation: useEffect runs side effects after the component paints; the other hooks serve different purposes.

questions.prompt: useReducer is preferable to useState when state transitions follow complex logic involving multiple sub-values.
questions.explanation: useReducer centralizes transition logic in a reducer function, which is cleaner for complex state.

questions.prompt: What does the dependency array [count] in useEffect mean?
options: The effect runs once on mount
The effect runs whenever count changes
questions.explanation: A non-empty dependency array re-runs the effect when any listed value changes.

questions.prompt: useContext allows a component to subscribe to a context without prop drilling.
questions.explanation: useContext reads the nearest Provider value directly, bypassing intermediate components.

questions.prompt: In a controlled component, where does the input's value come from?
questions.explanation: Controlled inputs derive their value from state; every keystroke updates state, which re-renders the input.

questions.prompt: Uncontrolled components use a ref to read the input's value at submit time rather than on every change.
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled inputs let the DOM own the state; you read the value via a ref when needed.

questions.prompt: When should you validate form input?
options: Both on change and on submit, depending on UX needs
questions.explanation: A common pattern is light validation on change for immediate feedback and full validation on submit.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of extracting data-fetching logic into a custom hook?
options: Reusable, testable logic that separates data concerns from UI
It removes the need for error handling
questions.explanation: Custom hooks encapsulate data logic so components stay focused on presentation and the hook is reusable.

questions.prompt: A custom hook that fetches data should handle loading, error, and success states.
questions.explanation: Exposing all three states lets the consuming component render appropriate UI for each.

questions.prompt: What pattern helps when an API request fails temporarily?
questions.explanation: Retry with exponential backoff handles transient failures gracefully before surfacing an error.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a single-page application (SPA) from a traditional website?
options: SPAs reload the full page on every navigation
SPAs update only the content that changes without full page reloads
SPAs require a server for routing
questions.explanation: SPAs fetch a single HTML shell and update the DOM via JavaScript, giving a fluid, app-like experience.

questions.prompt: React Router's <Link> component prevents full page reloads and uses client-side navigation instead.
questions.explanation: Link intercepts clicks and updates the URL via the History API, avoiding a server round-trip.

questions.prompt: How do you define a route parameter like :lessonId in React Router?
questions.explanation: Dynamic segments in the path string become parameters accessible via useParams().

questions.prompt: What does React.memo do?
options: Prevents re-renders when props haven't changed
questions.explanation: React.memo wraps a component and skips re-renders when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props.

questions.prompt: useMemo should be used to memoize every expensive computation, even if it runs only once.
questions.explanation: useMemo has its own overhead; it's only worth it when the computation is genuinely expensive and re-runs frequently.

questions.prompt: Which attribute on an element is essential for accessibility?
questions.explanation: The alt attribute provides text alternatives for screen readers; decorative images use alt="".

questions.prompt: What component is used to apply a custom theme in Material UI?
questions.explanation: ThemeProvider wraps the app and injects the theme object into all MUI components via context.

questions.prompt: Material UI's sx prop allows inline styling with theme-aware values.
questions.explanation: The sx prop accepts a style object that can reference theme tokens like spacing, colors, and breakpoints.

questions.prompt: Which MUI component is used to collect single-line text input?
questions.explanation: TextField is MUI's primary text input component, supporting labels, helpers, and validation states.

questions.prompt: What is a pull request primarily used for?
options: To propose changes for review before merging into a target branch
questions.explanation: A PR initiates code review and discussion before changes are merged into the main branch.

questions.prompt: GitHub Actions workflows are defined in YAML files stored in the .github/workflows directory.
questions.explanation: Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows; each defines triggers, jobs, and steps.

questions.prompt: Which branching strategy uses 'feature/', 'bugfix/', and 'main' branches?
questions.explanation: Git Flow uses structured branch prefixes and separate develop/release branches for organized workflow.

questions.prompt: What is npm primarily used for?
questions.explanation: npm is the Node Package Manager — it installs dependencies listed in package.json.

questions.prompt: Node.js is required to run a Vite-based React development server.
questions.explanation: Vite runs on Node.js; you need it installed to use npm and start the dev server.

questions.prompt: Which file in a Vite project specifies the single HTML entry point?
questions.explanation: index.html is the entry HTML file that loads the main.tsx script via a module tag.

questions.prompt: What does the 'npm run build' command typically produce?
options: A production-ready dist/ folder with optimized assets
questions.explanation: The build step bundles, minifies, and outputs static files to dist/ ready for deployment.

questions.prompt: Environment variables prefixed with VITE_ are exposed to the client-side code in a Vite project.
questions.explanation: Vite only exposes env vars prefixed with VITE_ to the browser; others remain server-only.

questions.prompt: What is DNS configuration used for in deployment?
options: Pointing a domain name to the hosting server's IP address
questions.explanation: DNS records map your custom domain to the host's IP so visitors reach your deployed site.

questions.prompt: Which type of test verifies that individual functions or components work correctly in isolation?
questions.explanation: Unit tests focus on the smallest pieces of code, testing each function or component independently.

questions.prompt: End-to-end (E2E) tests simulate real user interactions across the entire application stack.
questions.explanation: E2E tests drive a real browser to click, type, and navigate, verifying the full user flow.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of mocking in tests?
options: To replace real dependencies with controlled fakes for predictable testing
questions.explanation: Mocks substitute external dependencies (APIs, modules) so tests remain deterministic and isolated.

questions.prompt: A test pyramid recommends more E2E tests than unit tests.
questions.explanation: The test pyramid favors many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and very few slow E2E tests at the top.
